chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: Nobody cares about a great jazz writer
summary: Sauter and Kirchner talk about geniuses being remembered and Rod Levitt.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: He was a teacher, but I don't think that he never--of course writing is a little different, he never got the high C's that he should have, that he was reaching for, never got there. It's probably adequate enough; what I've heard was adequate. But I don't really think he made that cross over, but that's another thing. It's not quite like playing. In writing, you just can't be good; you've got to be a genius, it seems to be and if you're not, nobody cares, really. nobody wants to do it, although that's probably necessary for the next generation to pile it on, where somebody comes along and learns from that. I think it's probably not wasted, but the way we live they want geniuses;
the only people they remember are geniuses.
It's funny, about a year or so ago, do you know Rod Levitt?

He's a very good arranger, he had a wonderful octette, jazz octette in the sixties, and he's now a very successful commercial arranger, jingle writer, and he said something to the effect, you could get to be a great jazz writer and nobody cares.
